lessons.title: Two halves, no stopping
lessons.objective: You can explain how long a match is and why the clock does not stop.

payload.prompt: How long is a football match?

options.text: 80 minutes
90 minutes
100 minutes

explanation.correct: Right. Two halves of 45 minutes each, plus the referee adds stoppage time at the end.
explanation.incorrect: It's 90 minutes total: two 45-minute halves. The clock never actually stops though, so there's extra time added.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ninety minutes is what they call regulation time.

payload.prompt: Guess: how many extra minutes did the ref add today?

explanation.correct: Close. Refs usually add a few minutes at the end of the first half and often five or more at the end of the second, depending on injuries, goals, substitutions and delays.
explanation.incorrect: Added time varies, but a few minutes in the first half and around five or more in the second is common. It depends on how much time was lost to injuries, goals and delays.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five minutes added on, so there's still time for a winner.

payload.prompt: During a match, the referee stops the clock when the ball goes out. True or false?

options.text: True, the clock stops every time
False, the clock runs the whole 90 minutes
Only in the last 10 minutes

explanation.correct: Right. The clock keeps running even when play stops. Time is only added at the end.
explanation.incorrect: The clock never stops during a match. The referee tracks lost time and adds it at the end of each half.
explanation.sayThisLine: The clock's always running, that's why they add time on.

payload.prompt: Complete the match structure.
payload.template: A match has {{halves}} halves of {{minutes}} minutes each.

explanation.correct: Right. Two 45-minute halves make 90 minutes of regulation play.
explanation.incorrect: A match is two halves of 45 minutes each, for 90 minutes total.

lessons.title: What counts as a goal
lessons.objective: You can tell a goal from a near miss by the whole-ball-over-the-line rule.

payload.prompt: The whole ball crossed the line between the posts, no bounce before. Goal?

scene.alt: The ball is played forward and the whole ball crosses the goal line between the posts at waist height.

explanation.correct: Yes. When the whole ball crosses the whole line, it's a goal.
explanation.incorrect: If the whole ball crosses the whole line between the posts and under the crossbar, it is a goal.
explanation.sayThisLine: Whole ball over the line, that's a goal.

payload.prompt: Half the ball is over the line. Is it a goal?

options.text: Yes, any part crossing counts
No, the whole ball must cross
Only if a player touched it

explanation.correct: Correct. The whole ball must completely cross the whole line for it to count.
explanation.incorrect: The whole ball has to fully cross for it to count. A half-ball situation is not a goal.
explanation.sayThisLine: The whole ball, the whole line. That's the rule.

payload.prompt: Match the goal-related term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The whole ball completely crosses the goal line between the posts and under the crossbar.
The vertical bar at the corner of the goal that defines the width of the net.
The horizontal bar connecting the top of the goalposts.

explanation.summary: The goal is the frame and the space; a goal is when the ball goes fully through it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Between the posts and under the bar, that's a goal.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: That was so close, I thought it was in.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: A shot that nearly went into the goal
A player was very close to the opponent
The ball was very near the goal line but didn't cross it
A goal was scored by a narrow margin

payload.translation: The ball went very close to the goal but the whole ball didn't fully cross the line, so it wasn't a goal.

followUps.line: How much of the ball has to cross to count?
followUps.why: Tests understanding of the whole-ball rule.

followUps.line: Did the keeper make a good save?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you're unsure, ask if it went in or just missed.

lessons.title: Getting the ball back into play
lessons.objective: You can say who restarts play after the ball goes out.

payload.prompt: Match the restart to what caused it.

pairs.definition: Attacker put it over the touchline; the opponent restarts with hands over head.
Attacker put it over the goal line; the defending goalkeeper or defender restarts from the six-yard box.
Defender put it over their own goal line; attacker restarts from the corner arc.

explanation.summary: Who touched it last and which line it crossed decides the restart.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ball goes out, the other team restarts it.

payload.prompt: Tap the corner arc, where corner kicks are taken.

diagram.alt: A full pitch with the corner arc highlighted at each corner.

explanation.correct: Right. A corner is taken from the arc in the corner, and you can score straight from it.
explanation.incorrect: The corner arc is a small quarter-circle in each corner, where the ball is placed for a corner kick.

payload.prompt: The ball goes out off a defender's foot. Who restarts it?

options.text: The defender
The attacker
The goalkeeper

explanation.correct: Right. The team that did NOT touch the ball last restarts it.
explanation.incorrect: The attacking team restarts because the defending team put it out.
explanation.sayThisLine: Out off them, so we get the restart.

payload.prompt: A throw-in is taken with both hands over the head. True or false?

scene.alt: A player holds the ball above their head with both hands and throws it back into play from the touchline.

explanation.correct: Right. A throw-in must be taken with both hands over the head, and the feet stay on or behind the line.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a throw-in is taken with both hands over the head. If you throw it one-handed or underarm, it's not valid.
explanation.sayThisLine: Both hands over the head, that's the throw-in rule.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: We get a corner every time we push them back, and that's where we're dangerous.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Her team defends well
Her team wins many corners and scores from them
Her team attacks down the line
Corners are where her team's strength is

payload.translation: When her team pushes forward and the defenders clear it over the goal line, she gets a corner kick. Her team scores well from corner situations.

followUps.line: Do you have a good set-piece coach?
followUps.why: Shows you know corners are coached.

followUps.line: How many corner goals has your team scored?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't know the team, ask what their main goal threat is.

lessons.title: Free kicks and penalties
lessons.objective: You can explain direct vs indirect free kicks and when a penalty is given.

payload.prompt: Tap the penalty area (the 18-yard box).

diagram.alt: The attacking third showing the penalty area, six-yard box, and penalty spot.

explanation.correct: Right. A foul inside this area is a penalty kick.
explanation.incorrect: The penalty area is the larger rectangle; the six-yard box is inside it. Fouls in the penalty area are penalties.

payload.prompt: A defender deliberately holds an attacker. Direct or indirect free kick?

scene.alt: A holding foul in the middle of the pitch. The attacker is held by the shoulder.

explanation.correct: Direct. A holding foul is a direct free kick, so the shooter can score straight from it.
explanation.incorrect: Dangerous contact like holding, pushing or dangerous play is a direct free kick. You can score straight from it.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's a direct foul, he can just shoot it in.

payload.prompt: When is a penalty awarded?

options.text: A foul anywhere on the pitch
A foul by a defender in their penalty area
A foul by an attacker in their own half

explanation.correct: Exactly. A foul inside the defender's penalty area is a penalty kick from 12 yards.
explanation.incorrect: A foul by the defending team inside their own penalty area gives a penalty kick.
explanation.sayThisLine: Foul in the box, that's a penalty.

payload.prompt: Complete the penalty rule.
payload.template: A penalty is taken from {{distance}} yards out, with only the taker and the {{opponent}} involved.

explanation.correct: Right. A penalty is taken from the penalty spot, which is 12 yards from the goal line.
explanation.incorrect: Penalties are taken from 12 yards away, marked by the penalty spot, with just the taker and keeper.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: His arm was out, natural position or not, that's the debate.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: A handball incident at a penalty
Whether a handball foul was committed
The referee's positioning
Whether the arm position makes it a handball

payload.translation: A player's arm was raised or extended, and it's unclear if his body was made unnaturally bigger, which decides if it's a penalty.

followUps.line: Do you think it was a handball?
followUps.why: Invites her opinion on the controversial moment.

followUps.line: Was the ball coming from close range?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Handball is one of football's most debated calls; it's fine to ask what she thinks.

lessons.title: Points, tables and drama
lessons.objective: You can read a league table and explain what a win, draw and goal difference do.

payload.prompt: Complete the points rule.
payload.template: A win gets {{win}} points, a draw gets {{draw}}, and a loss gets {{loss}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Three for a win, one for a draw, zero for a loss. The table ranks teams by points.
explanation.incorrect: Three points for a win, one for a draw, none for a loss.

payload.prompt: Two Premier League teams finish level on points. What separates them first?

options.text: The total number of goals they scored
Goal difference (goals for minus goals against)
Who won when they played each other

explanation.correct: Right. In the Premier League, goal difference comes first, then goals scored. Some other leagues check head-to-head results before goal difference.
explanation.incorrect: In the Premier League the first tiebreaker is goal difference: goals scored minus goals conceded. Goals scored comes next. Other leagues can use head-to-head first, so it is worth checking the rulebook.
explanation.sayThisLine: Same points, but we're third on goal difference.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: Fourth clean sheet in a row, that back four is locked in.

payload.question: What does 'clean sheet' mean?

options.text: A fresh team sheet for the new season
A match with no goals allowed
When a team doesn't score
When a team doesn't concede

payload.translation: Her team hasn't let in a goal in the last four matches; the defence is playing well.

followUps.line: Is the goalkeeper getting a lot of action?
followUps.why: Shows you know defences need support.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't watch often, ask who's playing well lately.

payload.prompt: How are teams ranked in the league table?

options.text: By the number of wins they have
By total points, with goal difference as a tiebreaker
By goals scored

explanation.correct: Right. Points first (three for a win, one for a draw), then goal difference breaks ties in the Premier League.
explanation.incorrect: Teams are ranked by points earned. If two teams are level, the league's tiebreaker decides. In the Premier League that is goal difference first.

payload.prompt: Match the table terms.

pairs.definition: The total earned from wins and draws; ranks teams in the table.
Goals scored minus goals conceded; breaks ties when teams have equal points.
The total number of goals a team has scored in the season.

explanation.summary: The table uses points first, then goal difference, to decide final positions.
explanation.sayThisLine: We're level on points but they have the better goal difference.

lessons.title: Knockouts, extra time and shootouts
lessons.objective: You can follow a knockout tie, including two-legged ties and shootouts.

payload.prompt: Order the knockout tiebreak from start to finish.

items.why: Two halves of 45 minutes plus stoppage time.
Two 15-minute periods if level after 90 minutes.
Alternating penalties if still level after extra time.
If level after five each, one miss decides it.

explanation.correct: That is the path: 90 minutes, then 30 of extra time, then five penalties each, then sudden death.
explanation.incorrect: First 90 minutes, then two 15-minute periods of extra time, then a shootout with five penalties each, then sudden death.
explanation.sayThisLine: It went to sudden death and they finally scored.

payload.prompt: A two-legged tie: first leg 2-1, second leg 1-1. Who goes through?

options.text: The first team (won 2-1)
The second team (drew 1-1 at home)
It's 3-2 on aggregate, so the first team

explanation.correct: Right. It's 3-2 on aggregate (combined score), so the first team advances.
explanation.incorrect: You add the goals from both legs. If it's level on aggregate, extra time and penalties are played.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's 3-2 on aggregate so they're through.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: It'll go to penalties, I can't watch.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The match is heading for a penalty shootout
The referee will give out a lot of yellow cards
She is too nervous to watch the kicks
Extra time is about to start

payload.translation: After extra time, if it's still level, both teams take five penalty kicks each to decide it. She's nervous.

followUps.line: How many does each team get before sudden death?
Is your keeper good at penalties?
followUps.why: Asks a genuine question about her team's strength.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can say you find shootouts stressful too.

payload.prompt: A knockout match is 1-1 after 90 minutes. There will be extra time. True or false?

scene.alt: A tied match at 90 minutes in a knockout round. Neither team has scored the winner yet.

explanation.correct: True. A knockout match tied after 90 minutes goes to two 15-minute periods of extra time.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, in knockouts a tie means 30 minutes of extra time is played. If still level, it goes to penalties.
explanation.sayThisLine: Level after ninety, so it's extra time next.

payload.prompt: How many penalty kicks does each team get in a shootout before sudden death?

explanation.correct: Right. Five penalties each, then sudden death if still level.
explanation.incorrect: Each team gets five penalty kicks in the shootout. After that, if level, it goes to sudden death.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five each and then sudden death, whoever misses first loses.

lessons.title: Eleven, the bench and the armband
lessons.objective: You can explain who plays, how substitutions work and what a captain does.

payload.prompt: How many players start on the pitch per team?

explanation.correct: Right. Eleven on the pitch at the start: one goalkeeper and ten outfield players.
explanation.incorrect: Each team starts with 11 players on the pitch.
explanation.sayThisLine: Eleven on the pitch, and five subs they can use.

payload.prompt: Complete the substitution rule.
payload.template: Modern football allows up to {{num}} substitutions per team, made in no more than {{windows}} stoppages, plus half-time.

explanation.correct: Right. Five substitutions, made in up to three stoppages in play, with half-time as an extra chance that does not count as a window.
explanation.incorrect: The modern rule is five substitutions per team, spread over a maximum of three stoppages, plus the half-time break.

payload.prompt: Match the squad terms.

pairs.definition: The eleven players chosen to start the match on the pitch.
The area where substitute players sit during the match.
A player who enters the match during play, replacing another player.

explanation.summary: Teams have 11 starters and several subs; a manager can use up to five subs during a modern match.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's on the bench today but could come on in the second half.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: Only the captain is supposed to talk to the ref.

payload.question: Why is this rule important?

options.text: To stop players from arguing
Because the captain earns more money
To keep control and reduce dissent
To make the game faster

payload.translation: The referee wants to speak to only one player (the captain with the armband) to avoid chaos and dissent from multiple players.

followUps.why: Shows you know it's been emphasized recently.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't know the captain, ask who the leader is.

lessons.title: Scoring milestones fans cheer
lessons.objective: You can use hat-trick and brace correctly and know the fan talk around them.

payload.prompt: Match the scoring term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Two goals scored by one player in a single match
Three goals scored by one player in a single match
Three goals in a match: one right foot, one left foot, one header

explanation.summary: These terms celebrate individual goal-scoring feats in a single match.
explanation.sayThisLine: He got a brace in the first half and finished with a hat-trick.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: He got a hat-trick in the first half, absolutely ridiculous.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: Three goals in one match
A hat passed to him three times
Three assists
An unusually fast performance

payload.translation: One player scored three goals in just the first 45 minutes, which is exceptional.

followUps.why: Shows genuine surprise at the rarity.

followUps.line: What did the team do in the second half?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If it's unfamiliar, ask if that's a rare thing.

payload.prompt: A player scores two goals in a match. What is this called?

options.text: A brace
A hat-trick
A clean sheet

explanation.correct: Right. Two goals is a brace. Three goals is a hat-trick.
explanation.incorrect: Two goals in a match is called a brace. It's a step below a hat-trick.
explanation.sayThisLine: He got a brace today, that's two goals.

payload.prompt: Complete the definition.
payload.template: A {{term}} is when a team plays the whole match and concedes {{goals}} goals.

explanation.correct: Right. A clean sheet means no goals allowed; the team's defence kept them out.
explanation.incorrect: A clean sheet is a match where a team doesn't concede (allow) any goals.
